COLD WEATHER—PRO AND CON.—The
weather yesterday was unusually cold, and from
noon until midnight old Boreas aided in rendering
the atmosphere boisterously frigid in its character.
But cold weather is desirable for several reasons.
It is a fact well known, especially to the police,
and a philosophical one, that fewer arrests are
made during the prevalence of cold weather than
at any other of the year. The police records
yesterday showed but few arrests, most of which
were for violating Corporation ordinances.


The concurrent testimony of the lieutenants of
police proves that crime, particularly in its more
aggravated phases, prevails to much greater extent
in warm than in cold weather. This is easily
accounted for when it is considered that the cold-
ness of the weather prevents the perpetrators of
crime from venturing forth to pursue their avoca-
tions while they are comfortably sheltered from the
chilling blasts of winter. Another admirable feat-
ure of cold weather is that it makes pretty maid-
ens still prettier, giving a ruddy glow to their
cheeks, and brightness to their eyes which is
quite overpowering to the opposite sex. And then,
their jaunty hats propelled through the air by
sudden blast and caught after ludicrous chase by
some gallant masculine, who returns it with lifted
chapeau to the blushing fair—all goes to enliven
the street and make the avenue doubly attractive.


The boys likewise come in for a full measure of
enjoyment during the reign of cold weather. In the
way of skating on the pond, coasting and other
juvenile amusements of an innocent nature. City
car conductors, provided they don't "knock
down" to an unusual extent, render extraordinary
receipts, their cars being crowded with passengers,
who take refuge there in order to keep moderately
comfortable. Skate dealers reap harvest during the
cold season, the girls being afflicted with the
skating mania, and, of course, their
masculine admirers must indulge them to the ex-
tent of a pair of skates. Brown, who keeps the
coal yard, also prospers materially for the produc-
tion of calorie being in great demand, to ward off
Jack the Frost King. Best of all, the keen pure
air, supercharged with oxygen, induces sharp
appetite for good dinners, and renders culinary
luxuries more than ordinarily enjoyable. So much
for "pro"—and now a few words for "con."
Comfortably clad and residing in palatial man-
sions, the rich may laugh at the rude assaults of
old Boreas. But how of the poor! God help them!
Thinly clad living in almost shelterless hovels,
and in state bordering on starvation, without em-
ployment—how are they affected by the bitter
cold? Remember their suffering neighbors, parti-
cularly of this season, and open their purses
and observantly respond to the call of the needy.

The regular monthly meeting of this association
was held on Wednesday evening in the Council
Chamber of the City Hall, the president, Wm. R.
McLean, in the chair, and James H. Reed secretary.

well, John W. Murphy, Wm. G. Robinson, and
Alexander Patterson, as delegates from the Jour-
nymen Stone Cutters Association, were received
and the gentlemen admitted to seats.

ratified the new constitution adopted by the
assembly.


The resignation of Mr. Wm. H. Berger as cor-

On motion of Mr. Harrison, the chairman of the

pose of organisation.

this paper. The steamer Star made her first
trip from Sandusky to the Islands on Tues-
day. The first lake trip of the season from
this section, was made by scow belonging
to Mr. W. Hazen of Toussaint. She took a
load of lumber to Sandusky on Tuesday and
returned on Wednesday. A little diff-
iculty, between two persons in beer saloon
in this place, last Saturday, was quietly set-
tled. To avoid trouble, one of the parties
struck the other on the head with brass fau-
cet, causing him to feel that the weight of the
argument was against him. Then the victor
went quickly out through the back door, and
the other poor fellow had his head tied up.
Both parties were rather the worse for beer.
The man whose head was cut open, lives
near Genoa, and the striker's name is Slaugh-
terbeck. Good order prevailed during the
entire proceeding. We presume it is not
deemed breach of peace to hit a man with
a faucet for no arrests were made. A
Post of the Grand Army of the Republic is
likely to be established here, soon.

persons were elected Borough Officers in
Fostoria for the ensuing year: G. G. Nestle
rode, Mayor; N. P. Robbins, Recorder; E.
Foster, P. D.; Caples, J. L. Mickey, J. J.
Myers, J. C. Johnson, Councilmen.
The series of meetings that were in progress
at the London Church, two miles East of
Fostoria on the Tiffin road closed March 9th
1867. There were sixty conversions and
sixty accessions to the U. B. Church, making
in all one hundred and seventeen received
into the U. B. Church on Fostoria circuit
during the winter. On last Monday night
some person broke pane of glass out of the
window of Mr. Gladstone's grocery store
Fostoria, and took two sacks of flour.
The Order of Good Templars of Fostoria now

From the Findlay Jeffersonian: We learn
that a child, about five years old, in Benton,
met with an accident, that resulted in her
death. Some one had been chopping logs
near the residence of the child's parents, and
piling them up. He finished his work and
left one pile with a log lying across it in such
manner that very slight weight would
displace it and throw it down. The little
girl was playing about the pile and by some
means caused the log to fall upon her. The
mother of the child saw her and ran to relieve
her from her perilous position, but was un-
able to move the log, which was lying across
the girl's breast. Being deaf and dumb the
agonized mother could not give the alarm, and
seemed to be stunned. A neighbor saw her
and supposing that the log heap had fallen
upon her, came running to assist her. Un-
fortunately he did not see that the little girl
was under the log and stepped upon it. He
saw his mistake and immediately removed
the log from the breast of the child; but life
was extinct. We learn that fire occur-
red at Kansas Station, on the D. & R. R.
Railroad, on Tuesday last. The steam saw
mill, known as Sprouts mill, was burned to
the ground and large lot of lumber destroy
ed. The mill is a total loss, as no insurance

originated from some "live" ashes that were
taken up in a wooden vessel. It is understood that E. B. Wilson will enter upon
the duties of his office, as Collector of the
Fifth District, the 1st of April.

formed that the wife of our fellow-townsman
A. F. McCurdy, is one of the heirs of the
$75,000 Groves estate, in Holland, O.,
which so much has been said in the papers
of late. There are, so far as ascertained,
sixty five heirs who will come in for a share
so it will be a quite nice thing. We hope he
will soon get it, for he has promised to maxi
us a present of a suit of new clothes when he
does.


WOOD COUNTY.


From the Perrysburg Journal: On Friday
morning last, Judge McKenzie, of Lima, who
presided in the County-Seat Contest case
gave in his decision, to the evident satisfac-
tion of many, and to the marked chagrin and
gnashing of teeth of others. The learned
Judge held the election void in the follow-
ing townships—Bloom, Montgomery, Freedom,
Milton, Troy, Liberty, Jackson, on account
of defective certificates to the poll books, re-
turned by the Election Boards to the Clerk
of the Court of Common Pleas. In many in-
stances there were no certificates at all in re-
lation to the vote on the question of removal
and in others no certificates of the number
of voters voting at the election, and other mani-
fest defects, going to make up gross irregu-
larities. The Court found that there were 1,154
regular, legal votes cast for removal of the
county seat, and 1,899 legal votes against
removal, thus leaving a clear majority against
removal. Exceptions to the decision of Judge
McKenzie were noted, and it is the intention
of the counsel in the interest of Bowling
Green to carry the case up.

"but have no notion of selling him the property"

Two weeks later Squire Skinner entered the Doctor's office again. "Well Doctor," said he, "I wrote Tom I'd sell him that property for thousand dollars including the five acres of land. I did not think he'd take it for the buildings are pretty shabby; but he has accepted my terms, and sent me fifty dollars to bind the bargain, saying he will be here the last week in March to take deed of it. So you'd better be prepared to rent your office about that time," and the Squire in his turn, laughed at his wit.

"He can hire the shoemaker's shop around the corner cheaper," said the Doctor. "and it'll be more in his way of business here, probably," and the two both laughed together.

"So it appears that young Upton isn't going to begin practice here just at present," said Dr. Bragg to the Squire. "But he's a fool to buy that property, and lay out so much on it when he isn't going to use it. He always was full of foolish freaks."

stay in that country became acquainted with one of
her citizens, concerning whom very good story
was told. He had been to Congress and was noted
for the great care he took of his personal appearance. The faro dealers on the Mississippi river
boats were wont to carry the peculiar implements
of their profession in small mahogany boxes.


Our representative friend, upon a certain time,
having occasion to go up the river, took with him,
for state-room convenience toilet box, which for
a few minutes after getting on the boat he carried
in his hand. His advent was very cheering to the
souls of two or three Kentucklans on board, who
had been all day itching to jump at tiger,
thinking, from his foppish appearance and from
the box he carried in his hand, that he was a mem
ber of the sporting fraternity. After consultation
among themselves, one of the Kentuckians advan-
ced toward Mr. —, and in most affable tone
bade him good evening. The salutation was re-
turned courteously, and thus encouraged, Ken-
tucky proceeded to interrogate: ,


"When you going to open up, Stranger?"


"What did you observe, sir?" said the honora-
ble member, not precisely understanding the drift
of the remark.


"Ol open up, you know; when are you going to
give us show agin the animal?"


"I don't understand your allusion, sir, in the
least. I am entirely in the dark regarding your
meaning in asking such questions, sir," was an-
swered with dignity.


"Ol-playing the 'possum game are you! May,
be you think we ain't game for your gun," said
Kentucky, and as his companions came up, he ex-
hibited a large roll of bills, and added, "Thar ar
three such bundles in this crowd stranger, and Ken-
tucky boys ain't afeard to risk their money. Won't
you open up this evening, Stranger?"


Mr. — was growing angry; the passengers
were beginning to press around; and in voice
bursting with wrath, he asked:


"For whom do you take me, sir, and what do
you suppose is my business?"


"Take you for? What should we take you for
with that faro box? Maybe you mean to say you
are not sporting gentleman, and never heard of
sich a thing as tiger!"


A light began to break upon the mind of the as-
tonished gentleman from Arkansas. Anxious to
correct a misapprehension which he saw extended
to the passengers, he nervously unlocked his toilet
box, and displayed to the vision of the Kentuck-
ians his complement of combs and brushes, and
other adjuncts of the toilet in triumph.


Silence was observed for a moment on both sides,
Then the Kentuckans, with an air of disgust, turn
ed away simultaneously, as one of them muttered:


"Stranger, we thought you were sporting Gen-
tlemen! But if we had knowed you was barber,
we wouldn't have spoken to you."

BUILDINGS IN PROGRESS BY BALDWIN BROTHERS

Two or three days since we were shown through the new building of Mr. M. N. Gait now being erected on H street north, between Fourteenth and Fifteenth streets west. It has a large and handsome brown-stone front, four stories high, with high and roomy basement. The front doors are made of black walnut, and are heavy and beautiful. The vestibule is large and the inner doors are also large and composed of black walnut. In fact, all the woodwork of the first story, and the blinds at the front windows, from the first to the upper story, are manufactured from the best of black walnut. The first floor embraces a large hall, parlor, library, dining room, and large and conveniently-arranged closets and niches. To the dining room there is a large and handsome bay window, the woodwork of which is beautifully executed in black walnut. The floors of the dining room and hall are walnut and ash lumber alternated.

The second floor has several fine chambers, bath, waste-water, and heating apparatus rooms and a large sitting room in the back building. The wash stands are all walnut, with marble tops and present a neat and beautiful appearance. The closets and pantries are large and well arranged, containing little cupboards with marble tops, and a number of shelves.

The third story is furnished with about the same conveniences, and is trimmed throughout with grained oak, as is also the fourth story rooms. Above the latter is a large and well-arranged lookout, from which nearly every part of the city can be viewed, as well as a wide area of the surrounding country and the noble Potomac for miles away.

There are eighteen rooms above the basement, over all of the doors of which are transom lights, thus permitting the air to have free current. The gas, water, and heating apparatus extend to all parts of the building, and are most conveniently arranged. The windows, from the basement upwards, are of French plate glass, two panes to the window. In the basement there are three rooms: the front is a private billiard room; the next room for general convenience, and the back room contains the furnace, heating apparatus, gas, water pipes, &c. It is, in fact, the best arranged house in the city. The building will be occupied in about two weeks, by Mr. Gait and family, who now reside on Y street. The residence will stand as a sample of the good work that is executed by the Baldwin Brothers.

N. W. Gait & Co. four-story iron-front building, on Pennsylvania avenue above Eleventh street, is progressing towards completion, and the plasterer will soon commence operations on its walls.

The splendid iron front store of John T. Ellis, esq. on Pennsylvania avenue, between Ninth and Tenth streets, is now being trimmed out, and the walls are being handsomely frescoed, preparing, story to arranging the shelving. Mr. Ellis expects to occupy his new store, we learn, inside of two weeks.

On Four and a half street, between C and D streets north, the same firm are building, for Mr. John Purdy, a large three story brown-stone front residence with French roof. It will be a commodious building and will embrace all the improvements and conveniences of modern times. The carpenter work is now being done.

The DEFEAT OF JOHN T. FORD—John Ford so well known in this city, addresses his friends in Baltimore, concerning his defeat as a political candidate at the election in that city on the 23d instant:

To my Democratic and Conservative Friends in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Wards: I desire to return my grateful thanks for their kind support yesterday at the polls. It was gallantly fought—it took an army of officers with provost guard of whippers-in, to conquer us.

The precinct of the Twentieth ward, where I was announced and where the speaker belonged, that whoever voted for me would be prescribed hereafter from office—gave me a majority. In other precincts the threat had more efficacy, so that the voters loved Ford less, but once more, and enough of offices were promised faithful adherents to concern all the appointments to the West End, even if they were multiplied fourfold.

A youthful political indiscretion (known as nothingism, long since cancelled by better manhood) was brought against me, although at the same time the right hand man of the successful candidate, and his escort yesterday, was the head and front of that defunct order then; yesterday, his word was law, and in his clever brains victories were organized. Erroneous statements that the nomination was offered to me and I declined, and that I suffered my name to go before primary meetings are equally incorrect. When asked, I invariably replied that the nomination was offered, and that I would accept. When it was offered, I kept my word. I have been defeated, and I accept the situation as manager of public amusements instead of public affairs, with a strong personal conviction that "the grapes are sour."

If I could relate, humorously, the experiences of yesterday, and tell of the expedients of the blood-and-thunder fraternity in search for stamps, it would be laughable to the general reader and instructive to the future candidate. I escaped the fate of "the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thieves, who stripped and wounded him and departed, leaving him half dead," but I was because the past had its lessons.

And now, in parting from politics and political friends, permit me to follow recent example, and say:

"Good night, good night! parting is such sweet sorrow, That shall say good night till it be morrow."

JOHN T. FORD.

October 24th, 1867.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY—Frederick Buckner, Nathaniel Tyler, Daniel Webster and Richard Burnley had a hearing before Justice Tucker, at the First precinct station, charged with being drunk and disorderly. Frederick and Nathaniel not having the funds to pay their fines, were sent to the workhouse. Daniel and Richard paid a fine of $5 each.

Jesse Jackson was arrested by Officer Brenshaw, of the Sixth precinct, for disorderly conduct, and fined $5 by Justice Harper. William Togenny was arrested by Officer Wilson, of the Fifth precinct, for being drunk and disorderly, and fined $5 by Justice Harper. A Griss, for being profane, was fined $5 by the same Justice.

Owen McCauley, Sarah Brown and John Dudley made their appearance yesterday morning before Justice Walter, at the Seventh precinct station, charged with disorderly conduct.

Revenue for 11th District, who is
in custody at JEFFERSON, charged with the murder of
his late assistant Col. W. H. FOSSE.


The facts as they are related are as
follows: 11sley, in command of
the troops at this place, at the re-
quest of Mrs. Bosssey furnished
guard for the premises for several
nights until, at last, Mr. deem-
ing it no longer necessary, it was de-
continued. On Monday she had a
strange presentiment of evil, which
she communicated to one or two
officers so strongly that she was
pressed with it; thus, she requested
renewal of the guard, for some pro-
tection. On consultation with 11sley,
she determined that the
presence of one soldier would be
sufficient, who slept on mattresses on
back floors.


About the dawn of day, cries of
screams were heard at Mrs. Bosssey's
residence, which attracted the atten-
tion of the neighbors, and indeed
one of them went to over and see what
was the matter, which was a sight as
far as the eye could contemplate. There
lay the lady insensible and bleeding
from her blood. Some man in human
shape, had entered the premises and
had struck her a blow to the head,
breaking in her skull. The news
spread rapidly, bringing many to the
scene. The screams proceeded from
one of the children, who awoke and
found his mother in this sad condi-
tion. The soldier who was aroused
by the cries in the house, states that
he immediately felt for his gun,
which he had by his side, but
which had been taken away, and has
not since been found. Going to the
house, and seeing Mrs. Bosssey in this
condition, he immediately left for
camp to inform 11sley of it,
while some of the servants started to
call in the nearest neighbor.


No clue has yet been arrived at as
to who committed the deed.
None of the drawers were opened
and nothing was missing except a
small amount of money, $2 or $5,
which was in the pocket of Mrs.
Bosssey's dress, and a pound cake,
which she had baked for her hus-
band.


Various conjectures are made as to
the cause of the murder. Our own
impression is, that robbery was the
object. The night previously the
residence of Major Blanche had been
invaded, Mrs. Alexander's room en-
tered, and a valise, containing clothing,
and other articles, carried away.
During the last week, attempts had
been made to enter other houses.
The fact that the premises were
guarded by soldiers, unsuccessfully,
led to the belief that there was
considerable amount of money in the
house.


The house is long, with a front
on the south, with a gallery extend-
ing the entire length. Two windows
are, one on the South West and the other on
the South East. The robbers
probably entered on and exited through the
other. Whoever
committed the deed, was either well
acquainted with the premises or had
accomplices who knew the facilities
of everything.


The most severe measures were
at once taken by the sheriff and 11sley
to discover and arrest the
murderer. Runners were sent in
every direction, on all the public
roads, and a telegram was sent to
Jefferson to guard the ferry. Every
one unable to give a satisfactory
account of themselves were arrested
and brought to this place. In
consequence, a number of
spectacle persons were brought to
Marshall, who were immediately dis-
charged after investigations. Four of the negroes on Mrs. Bosssey's
place were also arrested and con-
fined. Thus far all efforts to dis-
cover the perpetrator of this outrage
has proved unavailing. The mys-
tery remains unsolved. The un-
fortunate lady, insensible from the
beginning, is slowly dying. This
is a distressing and horrible
sair, without a parallel in this
section.

Young, tax collector for this county,
sends us a couple of ears of corn which

their chunky appearance they look

inches in length, and 4 inches in
circumference, the other 12 1/2 in length
and 3 in circumference, and contains
upwards of thirteen hundred grains.

Young writes us that it is a new kind

man in the State who has any idea of it,
to whom he sends this. The ears sent us were
cleaned, but taken as they'd fall off
while picking fodder. Can any one
describe these specimens?

on Wednesday evening, the 18th inst. A
contract having been let by the Town Council (of which we mentioned in this paper two

weeks ago) to sink a well forty feet deep.

driven into the hole and large braces from

no hope was entertained for the rescue of

article_spellcheck: A large and fashionable congregation assembled this morning at the Unitarian church of Fourth and Twentieth street, known to popular parlance as "Ann Seals." The Rev. Dr. Bellows officiated in the usual liturgical service of the Unitarians—which was modelled very closely upon that of the Episcopalians. Having recited the usual morning invocation coupled with recitation to use Hebrew metaphor, of psalms and other sacred songs, the officiating clergyman read selections of texts from the Proverbs of Solomon; after which followed second invocation and the singing of hymn in duet. These services concluded, the reverend gentleman announced the subject of his discourse of the wise sayings of Solomon, viz. "A merry heart doeth good like medicine: but a broken spirit drieth up the bones." The general thesis of the sermon drawn out by way of exegetical comment, lesson and explanation from the text in short may be stated briefly: the enforcing of the duty of all religions to maintain proper pleasantness of temper and hopefulness of disposition. By way of ordium the speaker preceded with somewhat critical explanation of the verse quoted. The meaning of the verse was argued by the speaker, that a merry heart did good in the place of medicine or was equivalent thereto. It was known that many forms of disease were peculiarly exaggerated in symptom by moroseness and dependency of disposition; while pleasantness, hopefulness and cheerfulness made opposite effects. There is a sort of sympathy between the mental and physical man, which could not be too carefully regarded, since it was the pivot upon which many bodily ailments revolved. There was, however, a distinction between hopefulness as disposition, both of which in day life matters are of simple duty, and that inordinate merriment and laughter which the Bible everywhere condemned as an element of exceeding weakness of mind. It said in another passage that the laughter of fools is like the crackling of thorns under a pot—sound, without sense or reason—the simple crackling of folly and nothing more; still even this could not be utterly condemned, for there are many persons who knew better, and even the pleasant and silly laughter of folly was preferable to the moroseness which people affected as an element of piety. The morose person made himself disagreeable to as with whom he came in contact, and the speaker could specify no greater duty of religious people than endeavour to make religion attractive and winning. If the laughter of fools was like cracking of thorns under a pot, the moroseness of the monk was like those thorns when too wet and soggy in a fire. Many people are driven away from the Saviour by the moroseness and austerity of affected piety by many of his disciples who thus, though perhaps unconsciously, were more instrumental in doing harm than good to the cause in which they were engaged. He did not aim to advocate the habit of boisterous laughing which is simply the cracking of thorns; but he did want to be understood advocating that well-balanced serenity, which is good medicine, not only to the body, but to the soul. From this exordium the speaker proceeded to explain at length his views concerning the duty of maintaining proper and pleasant serenity of disposition, concluding with exhortation to all to keep in all the concerns of life hope and a glad heart. The length of days is joy and merriment, but a broken spirit will dry up the bones.

One day as he sat by her in a playful mood (Captain Lance being asleep in an adjoining room) he turned her work box over, strewing its contents all about the table.

He took up a carved ivory card case and examined it curiously.

"That was a present from Hong Kong. Is it not beautifully cut?" Milly asked.

There was a flush upon her cheek as she spoke. He had opened the card case, which was deemed, perhaps, too good for use indeed. Milly had few friends upon whom to call and leave cards, and her case contained none; but a photograph fell out.

"That is my cousin, Mark Lance. He was who sent me the card case. He represents a mercantile house at Hong Kong." Her voice trembled a little as she volunteered this explanation.

"Has he been out there long?" the doctor asked, quietly.

"He came home two years ago. He went out first of all quite young. A very good looking young fellow."

The doctor closed the card case. He next took up a small, carefully tied packet.

"Those are Mark's letters," said Milly, rather breathlessly. "He generally writes about every other mail. But late, however, he has not been so regular. No letter came from him last week, but no letter came."

The doctor looked thoughtful. Had not something like a sigh escaped her as she said that no letter had come? Did she then long so very much to have tidings of her cousin? He turned the letters over and over, passing them in his hand.

"I see they are addressed to you, Milly," he said. There was further inquiry in the expression of his face.

"Would you like to read them?" she asked, simply. "Mark writes very amusing letters. He gives such a capital account of his life at Hong Kong. I think it would amuse you to read them."

"No, thank you, Milly." And he pressed her hand tenderly, as he gave her back the letters. For few moments he had doubted her; but he dismissed his doubts. Still he could not repress a feeling of jealousy in regard to this cousin of Milly's—this Mark Lance. It was comfort to reflect, however, that Hong Kong was very long way off.

WESSING, CAMPBELL AND COOPER.


A communication in a late number of
the Murfreesboro Monitor assails the
Hon. Wm. B. Campbell and Hon. Edmund
Cooper for tameness in their course as
Conservative members of Congress, and
as guilty of a dereliction of duty to their
constituents, in not replying by speech to
the assaults made by Radical Congress
men on the southern people. The writer
does great injustice to these gentlemen,
and shows himself poorly informed in re-
gard to the condition of things at Wash-
ington.


There are two reasons why these gen-
tlemen have not pursued the course indi-
cated as proper by the critic of the Moni-
tor. In the first place, it has been next
to impossible for them to do so. The
Radical majority in the House of Repre-
sentatives is as arbitrary and tyrannical
in the construction of the rules of that
body, and as exclusive against the Con-
servative members; and the special rules
and the general rulings of Speaker Colfax,
are as adverse to their rights as the body is in the treatment of the
great political questions involving the
rights of the Southern people. Under
this partisan strictness, it is difficult and
frequently impossible for Conservative
members to demand the ayes and noes.
To obtain the floor for a speech or so min-
ute in debate is a rare opportunity for a
Conservative member. The programme
of the majority is to push their
measures through under the previous
question and by every system of legis-
lative forcing that can be resorted to—to
stifle all debate. We are informed that
a list of the members is kept by the
speaker containing the names of those
who have previously signified a desire to
speak to the House, and he decides that
they can only have the privilege of the
floor in regular turn. The large prepon-
derance of Radical members, under this
practice, effectually excludes a Con-
servative from the right of extended speech
except when, by unusual good fortune
one may be able to secure it. This rigi-
d and partial system is violative of the con-
stitutional rights of members, and con-
verts the House from a deliberative body of
representatives of equal constituencies
into a caucus of the majority whose vote
controls the action, and who monopolize
the right of speech. It is one of the eva-
dences of the degeneracy of the times
and shows how far we have drifted from
the landmarks of the better time. But
it is true, nevertheless, and exempts
Conservative members from the charge of
lack of courage and fidelity to duty in
meeting Radicals to debate.


Secondly, it is of questionable exe-
pediency for Conservative members to in-
duce answers to the assaults of Radi-
cal congressional slang whanging against
the Southern people. They are insens-
itive to argument and deaf to appeal.
Any tartness of reply is likely to be con-
strued as designing disloyalty, and would
only be used as pretext for the scheme
of usurpation which they contemplate.

In the meantime my coffee was foaming over, and the rolls were burning to coals, and every instant the stove, which I had literally crammed with wood, was increasing its heat. I felt as if I should go mad. Every attempt made to rescue my supper left its mark upon my poor hands; and, to cap the climax, in the very heat of the fray there came a rap at the door. I smoothed my hair and wiped the perspiration from my face and I hurried out. The visitor was no other than aunt Debbie. If I ever gave utterance to anything like profanity in my heart, I feel sure that infinite Justice will not hold me accountable; for there are moments in life, I think when we sin involuntarily—sin because our souls are too weak, too sorely tried—help it.

Aunt Debbie followed me into the parlor, removed her shawl and bonnet, smoothed down her silk apron, and took out her roll of knitting.

"I heard Dorcas had left you," she said, in her pleasantest, even voice, "and I thought I'd drop in and see if YOU wanted help."

"No, no." I broke out passionately, "I can do well enough myself. I'm cooking supper now. Sit down here please; Owen will be home directly."

She acquiesced, and I hurried back to the kitchen. Owen's pointer was helping himself to the scattered trout, I gave him a punch that sent him limp out on three legs, and then rushed at the stove. The fire had gone down; and the foaming coffee subsided and the heavy, black topped rolls smoked in the oven. But I had no time to waste in repining. It was almost six o'clock, and my husband was a punctual man.

I went to work and gathered up the broken fish, placing them on a dish and peeling off the burnt skin; then selected the best of the rolls, and set about making Spanish buns. I had seen Dorcas make them, and I followed her example to the letter. As the stove was moderately warm, they baked pretty fairly, and I dried my eyes and began to set the table with something like reviving hope. Six o'clock found everything in readiness, and my handsome husband in his seat with his old friend on one hand, and aunt Debbie on the other.

"These are capital trout, Wat," he said, as he helped himself to them. "I ordered them purposely when I heard you were in town. Do them justice now; and take a roll—my wife is famous for making good bread."

I could hear my heart palpitating, and my hand trembled so that I could scarcely pour out the muddy, unsettled coffee. Mr. Seymour put out his small, delicate hand, and took a roll, broke off its black top, glanced at its heavy, spongy middle, and pushed it aside. It was rather heavy, he thought, and he was compelled to avoid everything indigestible. He was so prone to dyspepsia. Owen swallowed a bitter mouthful of burned trout with look of excessive annoyance.

"The rolls are heavy," he said; "your yeast must have failed, Mag; but try buns, Wat, Mag makes prime buns."

Mr. Seymour took one, tasted it, and laid it beside his roll. Owen, noticing bad taste in one, so looked up in utter astonishment.

"Why, Mag?"

"Well, what now?" I retorted, petulantly.

"You've made a mistake, child," said aunt Debbie, quietly; "you've put salt in your buns instead of sugar. Wait a moment, Mr. Seymour, till I slice some cold bread."

She rose with genteel dignity, while I, utterly unable to control my feelings, burst into tears.

"Maggie," said my husband, severely, "if you're going to act like this, you'd better go to your room."

I needed a second hint. The next instant found me in my chamber, and the door double locked. I was too deeply hurt, too much mortified, too angry to be reasonable; so I threw myself on the rug before the fire, and lost myself into a fit of nervous headache. CORRESPONDENCE.


WASHINGTON, September 22. The follow-
ing correspondence has passed between
Governor Orr of South Carolina, and Gen-
eral Sickles, relative to the removal of the
latter:


EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT OF SOUTH CAROLINA,
COLUMBIA, September 7th, 1867.
To Gen. D. L. Sickles, Charleston, S. C.


SIR: I have learned from the public
press, although I have received no official
notice of the fact, that you have been reliev-
ed from the command of the Second Mill-
itary District, embracing this state and
North Carolina, and that by order of the
President Major Gen. Canby has succeeded
to the same.


I desire to express to you the great regret
which I feel personally and officially, at
the course taken by the President and his
advisers in this matter. There are many
of the orders which have been issued by
you since the passage of the reconstruction
bills in March last which did not meet my
approval; but it is due to you and your off-
icial action that I should bear voluntary tes-
timony to the wisdom and success of your
administration, and to express the opinion
that the almost unlimited powers with
which you were invested by the acts of Con-
gress have been exercised with moderation
and fairness. Your general orders, No.
10, for this state are concerned, were,
last spring, in my opinion, absolutely necs-
sessary, looking to the impoverished condition
of the country, the shortness of the pro-
vision and staple crops of last year, to the
general pecuniary distress prevailing the
country, and to the necessity of protecting
the small means of farms and planters at
that time from the process of courts. They
were thereby enabled to subsist their fami-
lies and grow the present crop.


This crop promises to be many respects
and in many sections of the state the most
important and largest that has been grown
for several years, and when harvested you
could, without hazard or apprehension, have
executed your purpose, as declared to me,
of modifying general orders No. 10, so that
creditors could have enforced their demands
without producing general distress, if things
were not worse.


It is also due to you to say, that in my
judgment, if general orders No. 10 had not
been issued last spring, very considerable
increase in the number of troops in this
State would have been necessary to have
been stationed at many of the courthouses
to have preserved the public records from
destruction and insure the safety of sher-
iffs in executing civil process in their hands
which they had been ordered to levy by
thoughtless and heartless creditors. In my
opinion, general orders No. 10 received the
approval of a very large majority of the
citizens of South Carolina, and your gen-
eral administration as commandant of the
district is approved by a majority nearly as great.


In all the official intercourse which we
have had, I beg to tender you my thanks for
the uniform kindness and courtesy with
which I have been treated personally, and
for the disposition you have always mani-
fested to make the burdens of the military
government as light upon the people whom
I represent as it were possible under the
circumstances. I have not the pleasure of
a personal acquaintance with your suc-
cessor, General Canby, but hope that my off-
cial relations with him may be marked with
the same harmony and kind feeling which
have characterized our official intercourse
for nearly two years past. I have the hon-
or to be, General, very truly and respect-
fully, your friend and obedient servant,


JAMES F. ORR,


Governor of South Carolina.


The following is the reply of General
Sickles to Governor Orr:


WASHINGTON, Sept. 18, 1867.


Sir: Your Excellency's letter of the 7th
inst., was forwarded to me at New York,
and received on the 11th. The cordial
terms in which you are pleased to refer to
our official and personal relations during
my service in the Carolinas are gratefully
appreciated. In my successor, Brevet
Major-General Canby, you will meet an
officer whose ample experience and distin-
guished services have justly commended
him to the confidence of the Government.


In view of the announcement already made
by General Canby, adopting and confirming
the orders heretofore in force in the Second
Military District, it is not probable that
any change in the conduct of affairs will
result from the change in command. In my
retirement, it is a source of much gratifi-
cation to compare the present condition of
South Carolina with that which I found in
assuming command in the autumn of 1866.


The system of free labor has been suc-
cessfully inaugurated. The emancipated
blacks have been invested with civil rights
by the voluntary act of your legislature.
The tranquility and order which have been
maintained attest the general desire of all
classes of the people to observe the obliga-
tions of good citizens. An abundant har-
vest has rewarded industry. Grain is now
exported from Charleston. Registration
has proceeded almost to completion without
commotion or tumult, or any serious inter-
ruption of the ordinary occupations of the
people. Since October, 1866, the courts of
the United States and of the States have
exercised nearly all their powers without
hindrance.

the Representatives of the States of this
Union, who excluded from the Legislative
halls the representatives of ten States, are
laboring to subvert our government, we
rejoice in the fact that the Supreme Court
of the United States, by its recent decis-
ions in favor of the rights of American
citizens, has proved that that august tri-
bunal will perform, without fear or favor,
its high and solemn duties.


Resolved, That our cordial thanks are
due, and are hereby rendered to Presi-
dent Johnson, for his manly course in re-
sisting unauthorized Legislation and ad-
vocating the rights of all the States to their
Congressional representation, and that we
will unitedly sustain him in these his just
and patriotic acts.


Resolved, That labor is the basis of all
the material of prosperity and the great
creator of wealth, and that its interests
should always be favorably regarded by
our legislature; that the laborer should
have time for mental and moral culture,
and for healthful recreation, and that we
therefore heartily sympathize with the
laboring class in their endeavors to reduce
the legal standard of a day's labor, and de-
clare ourselves in favor of making eight
hours per day a legal day's labor, in all
mechanical and manufacturing pursuits,
in the absence of any agreement to the
contrary between contracting parties.


Resolved, That the over-working of chil-
dren in factories is an act of cruelty, de-
priving them of the proper means of edu-
cation, and undermining their health, and
that all employers in factories should be
forbidden under suitable penalties, from
working said children more than eight
hours per day.


Resolved, That all attempts on the part
of employers to reduce their workmen to a
condition of political slavery by coercing
their votes, should be held up to the ex-
crescence of freemen, and, if possible, frus-
trated by legislative action.

and embodies in itself all of those principles that
make their performances so popular. His troupe
of actors are unsurpassed as comedians, eques-
trians and acrobats, and the animals almost rival
ed their masters by their attractions.


The company arrived yesterday on the Eliza
Hancor, and the line of march was instantly taken
up for the Citadel Green, where preparations had
been made for their reception. The first grand
matinee takes place to-day, and both that and the
night performance will repay a visit.


THE U. S. STEAMER HARRIET LANE.—This vessel
which was among the first constructed steamers
for Revenue service, having been built some years
before the war, and which was considered some-
what celebrated in her day for speed and model,
arrived here from Havana, yesterday. The Har-
riet Lane has had something of a history, having
been among the first blockaders off this port when
the war began, and she was afterwards employed
in the Gulf and was captured in the harbor of
Galveston by the Texans, who, by bold dash, cap-
tured the Lane and several other craft. She was
afterwards employed by the Confederates and was
found in Havana when the war broke down, and
has again come into the possession of the United
States. She is in charge of the officer who com-
manded her when first built Capt. JOHN FAUNCE.
She looks somewhat rusty, and wants consider-
able repairs to make her appearance and speed
what it was of yore. She was ACCOMPANIED by the
U. S. Revenue steamer Hugh McCROCH and the
steamer Pelican.


NUISANCE.—The city ordinance prohibiting the
obstruction of the sidewalks has been frequently
evaded, and the citizens put to considerable in-
convenience on this account. This is particularly
the case on the prominent thoroughfares, and the
crowds who daily throng those streets are often
compelled to make wide detours in order to avoid
the distractions on the pavement. Several par-
ties, who have been detected violating the law on
this point, have been reported and fined, but the
nuisance still continues and the community suffers.
Many of the stores and private houses have their
cellar entrances on the sidewalk, and when they
receive coal or wood the load is dumped upon the
pavement, instead of in the street. Aside from
the inconvenience caused by the barrier, the dirt
and dust are very disagreeable and damaging to
both clothes and temper. The ordinance requires
that these distractions should be immediately re-
moved, and if allowed to remain on the sidewalk
beyond certain period, the parties transgressing
should be liable to fine. A proper regard to the
requirements of this law would result in a great
benefit to those who are now annoyed and delayed
by these barriers, and few cases reported by the
police would be a warning that the city ordinances
cannot be violated with impunity.

A HOT TIME IN THE SOUTH.

At this moment the most profound quiet
pervades all the communities of the South.
Not much as hostile word to the United
States is heard anywhere. A people
who were but few years ago in arms, and
whose resolute valor challenged the admi-
ration of the world, are now governed with
most difficulty by a handful of troops, and
would be just orderly and non-resistant
if all those troops were removed. They
have submitted to the tremendous penalties
imposed upon them without murmur. If
they have erred they have bitterly paid for.
The flower of their population lies in a
bloody grave. They have been stripped
of possessions equal in value to the national
debt of the United States. They have
complied with every requisition which the
President of the United States announced
as a condition for their restoration to the
government. They have seen the freed
man excited to deeds of violence and insult,
amidst an intoxicant bestiality which
may thus be engendered, many among them
entertain apprehensions of most fearful out-
breaks from the effects of the demoniac
counsels which are insidious—breathed in
to the ears of the blacks by fiends in human
form. Excluded from office, and their
leading men disenfranchised, they have seen
suffrage forced upon their former slaves by
those who do not permit coloured men
among themselves to exercise it. Amidst
all this they have displayed heroic for-
titude and patience which challenges admi-
ration in any heart that is capable of sym-
pathy. They do not even in the most part, display disposition to
assist the discussion of those questions
in relation to the transfer of their military
commanders which elsewhere have caused
so much excitement and animosity. Their
journals declare that to them it is a matter
of little moment what officer directs
reconstruction. Yet there are radical
presses which are only stimulated by
the noble spectacle of subversion and li-
berance to cry for fresh vengeance up-
on them, to declare that they have not been
punished enough, and that nothing but
unlimited injustice will make them loyal.
It is obvious that to such a spirit is to de-
stroy the entire policy of this government,
toward the Southern states. If they are
held responsible and are to be scourged
for contumacies outside their borders,
then their organs of public opinion express
disdain at responsibility for the same,
if idle to hope for proper restoration of the Union. The pleasing illusion to which
patriotic hearts so tenaciously cling may
well be banished at once, and the Ame-
rican people learn, like the South, to ac-
cept the situation, which is henceforth. If
such counsels prevail, to be the permanent
suggestion and alienation in the lately con-
quered States, accompanied by the African
possession of their governments, the control
of the legislation of the whole country by
the introduction of the same element into
our national councils, and the chronic de-
rangement of labor, commerce, and every
source of individual and national wealth
and prosperity in States which were once,
and are capable of being so again, the
chief foundation of the trade and revenue
of the nation.
